why: Father and son. Leopold (1719-1787) wrote the violin treatise and the Kindersinfonie; Wolfgang (1756-1791) is his son.
Sisters, and co-authors: Mildred wrote the tune of 'Good Morning to All' and Patty the words. The credit names them both because both are owed it.
No relation. Joe Hill (1879-1915) was the Swedish-American labour songwriter; Mildred Hill (1859-1916) an American composer and organist.
No relation, as above. Hill is an ordinary surname and this pair will keep recurring.
Husband and wife. Both composed, both are in the catalogue under their own names, and neither is a spelling of the other.
Father and son. The family fills this report on its own; every one of them is a separate composer.
No relation. Robert Franz (1815-1892) wrote Lieder; Ignaz Franz (1719-1790) was a priest who wrote the hymn 'Grosser Gott, wir loben dich'.
Father and son. Alessandro (1660-1725) wrote the operas, Domenico (1685-1757) the keyboard sonatas.
No relation and different continents: Charles Wood (1866-1926) was Irish, Abraham Wood (1752-1804) an American singing-school composer.
No relation. Aaron Williams (1731-1776) compiled English psalmody; Vaughan Williams is a double-barrelled surname that happens to end in the same word.
Two English composers who are genuinely confused for one another and are not related: Sir Frederick Bridge (1844-1924) of Westminster Abbey, and Frank Bridge (1879-1941), Britten's teacher.
No relation and three centuries apart: Robert White (c.1538-1574) was a Tudor church composer, Maude Valérie White (1855-1937) a Victorian songwriter.
Mother and daughter. Amelia (1838-1903) published under the initials A. L.; Liza (1862-1918) wrote the song cycles.
Two composers whose names really do differ by one letter, and neither is a misspelling: Jacobus Handl or Gallus (1550-1591) was Slovenian, Handel (1685-1759) German.
Bach and Beach differ by a letter and by everything else. Amy Beach (1867-1944) was American.
No relation. Scott Hayden (1882-1915) wrote rags with Scott Joplin.
As above: the one-letter surname test pairs Bach with Beach, and there are several Bachs.
Two American singing-school composers whose surnames differ by a letter. Both are real and both are in the catalogue.
Two early American composers, not one. Moors and Moore are separate surnames.
Nothing in common: Giaches de Wert (1535-1596) was a Franco-Flemish madrigalist in Mantua, Elisha West an American psalmodist.
Greger and Reger differ by a letter and by person: Luise Greger (1862-1944) wrote songs, Max Reger (1873-1916) the organ works.
No relation. Giovanni Gabrieli (c.1554-1612) was Venetian; Virginia Gabriel (1825-1877) an English songwriter.
The classic confusion, and two people: Kuhnau (1660-1722) preceded Bach at the Thomaskirche, Kuhlau (1786-1832) wrote the sonatinas every piano student meets.
Weber and Webern are a letter apart and a century: Weber (1786-1826) wrote Der Freischütz, Webern (1883-1945) the Op. numbers of the Second Viennese School.
Beach and Leach differ by a letter. James Leach (1762-1798) was an English psalmodist.
As above; the Smith spellings pair with each other and with Smyth, and all three are separate composers.

Different names as well as different people: Clarence 'Pinetop' Smith (1904-1929) was an American boogie-woogie pianist; Dame Ethel Smyth (1858-1944) an English composer and suffragette. Paired only because the check compares surnames a letter apart.
A shared surname and nothing else. John Stafford Smith (1750-1836) wrote the tune that became the American anthem; Clarence Smith was a Chicago boogie-woogie pianist a century later.
